Extract 1.
Questions 1-12.
You hear a neurologist talking to a patient who has had a traumatic incident.
For questions 1-12, complete the note with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello Jack, my name is Dr Faro and I'm here to conduct neurological assessment. How are
you today? I'm doing okay, nice to meet you. So they tell me you've just had an accident
playing football. Do you know how long ago the accident happened? Yes, just about six
hours ago, I crashed into another player. They tell me I hit the right side of my head against
his knee, but I don't remember any of it. He must have jumped pretty high for his knee
to hit my head.
Yes, I can see here that you then fell to the ground and were unconscious for 20 to 30
seconds. So you continue to experience amnesia about the event?
Yes, I mean, I remember running towards the guy and then nothing black. But then I woke
up later and felt absolutely fine for a while. I mean, I was chatting with the nurse and trying
to convince her to let me go home. So after you arrived at the first facility, you had
a generalised motor seizure and were given lorazepam to stop it. And I can see the CT
scan done then was unremarkable. I can see now that you are having slight psychomotor
slowing and some slurred speech. This may be because of the lorazepam. How are you feeling
in general. I'm a little nauseous. Also, I have a headache, but I mean, that is probably
to be expected, right? I mean, I hit my head. Maybe. But I want to get another CT, a non-contrast
CT of the cranium, and to keep you under observation as deterioration can be quite rapid in these
cases. In what cases? What do you mean deterioration can be rapid?
described a loosened period before your seizure, which is a classical presentation of an epidural
hematoma. Also, the fact that you then had a seizure and are showing a downward course
with more neurologic problems is another sign that concerns me, and the symptoms you just
described to me are also associated with this condition.
Okay, but what is an epidural hematoma? An epidural hematoma refers to the accumulation
of blood between the inner table of your skull and the outer-dural membrane, which is the
outermost layer of dense connective tissue surrounding your brain and spinal cord.
This condition is generally caused by a traumatic event involving a blunt object such as getting
hit in the head by someone's knee while playing football.
It often results in an overlying fracture of the skull.
It is the blood vessels in close proximity to the fracture that are the source of the
hemorrhage or bleeding.
I do need to tell you that there are other possibilities.
What other possibilities? Are they worse?
Other possibilities are a subarachnoid hemorrhage and subdural hematoma.
For these two, a loosened period is not expected,
but the CT will help us determine what your condition is.
For now, the most likely diagnosis is epidural hematoma.
Does it mean permanent damage?
I mean, will I be able to play football again?
I mean, my mum is already going to be pretty upset
with me about this injury.
Generally not, because the underlying brain
is usually minimally injured.
Prognosis is excellent if we treat it aggressively.
Also, you were brought in right away,
which increases the chance of a good outcome.
Of course, it also depends on what type
of epidural hematoma you have.
As for playing football again,
we can talk about that later.
I really hope I can continue to play.
I mean, I'm not that good, but I love the game.
Like I said, we can talk about that later, but first.
This is a benchmark education solution sample test paper.
Extract two, questions 13 to 24.
You hear a doctor in the A&E talking to a patient with chest pain.
For questions 13-24, complete the notes with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello Mrs. Frank, my name is Dr. Norman, how are you doing today?
Um, not so well. I mean why else would I come to the A&E at midnight?
Yes, you do have a point. So according to what you reported when you checked in, you
are experiencing acute chest pain. Is this the first time you've had this type of pain?
I've experienced occasional stabbing chest pain over the last two years, but it usually
goes away fairly quickly after a second or two.
And has that pain been in the right or left side of the chest?
It's usually on the left side of the chest, but sometimes the position changes.
Hm, generally cardiac pain lasting a second or two is not significant.
So what about today's acute pain?
When did it start?
It started about 4 hours ago at 8pm and has been persistent since then.
It is here in the centre of my chest.
And what about other symptoms?
Are you experiencing shortness of breath or heart palpitations?
Nothing like that.
It does feel a bit better when I sit up and lean forward.
Okay, I see.
Speaking of feeling better, did you take anything for the pain?
Um, yes, at 9pm, about 1 hour after the pain started. I took 2 parcetimal, but it didn't
seem to make any difference.
So let's just talk a bit about family history. Do you have any history of cardiac disease
in your family?
Yes, my dad had a myocardial infarction at 51 and also had a high cholesterol level.
Hmm, well, that certainly increases the risk of heart disease, but I see no other risk
factors evident so far.
Okay, so have you had any other illnesses recently?
Um, yeah, about two weeks ago I had an upper respiratory tract infection.
It lasted for about four to five days.
What symptoms did you have at that time?
The normal ones, you know, sore throat, blocked nose, sneezing.
Also a really bad cough.
The whole house was set with the same thing, my husband and two kids.
So, I've taken a look at your electrocardiogram, and I think I have an idea of what is going
on.
You say that your pain gets better when you sit forward.
This indicates a type of pain originating in the pericardium, the membrane that encloses
the heart.
Those two things combined with your recent upper respiratory tract infection points to
pericarditis with a viral atiology.
Hmm, okay, so what is that exactly? Is something wrong with my heart?
So pericarditis is swelling and inflammation of the membrane surrounding the heart. In
many cases of pericarditis the cause is unknown but one common cause is viral which can be
caused by a cold or pneumonia.
So is this serious? I mean, will I need to be admitted to the hospital?
No, I'm not recommending that to be admitted at this time. There is some risk for bleeding
into the pericardial space but for now I'm going to recommend rest and NSAIDs.
You need to get another electrocardiogram in four days, by that time your symptoms should
have cleared up and we will want to make sure that the ECG shows that everything has been
resolved.
Right is the end of part A. Now look at part B.
Part B. In this part of the test, you'll hear six different extracts. In each extract,
you'll hear people talking in a different healthcare setting.
For questions 25 to 30, choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what

Well, what a long day.
Yes, Dr Phillips.
There have been quite a few long days since that practice down the road closed all of

Definitely.
I mean, we have taken on an additional 3,500 patients.
Yes.
We thought it was going to be a temporary situation.
But we have only been able to relocate about 500 of those patients to other practices.
Yes, and some of the new patients have complex health needs.
I mean, we used to have a waiting time well below the national average, but now our patients

Yes, and I have noticed that many of the doctors are experiencing their own stress-related

I mean, what can we...
You hear a trainee doctor asking a senior doctor about a patient's chest x-ray.
Now read the question.
Dr James, I have a question about the 19-year-old boy's diagnosis.
Okay, have you taken a look at the chest x-ray?
Yes, I have.
I can see that both upper lobes are marked with ring and tubular shadows, representing
thickened bronchial walls.
Isn't this finding consistent with the diagnosis of bronchiactasis?
Yes, but the prominence of the pulmonary arteries in the chest x-ray indicate a degree of pulmonary
hypertension.
Also, the medical history is quite important in this particular case.
The patient has a long history of repeated chest infections.
Yes, I hadn't considered that part.
Question 27.
You hear part of a training about sports nutrition.
Now read the question.
So, today's training will examine how poor nutritional intake affects an athlete's ability
to train, recover from training, compete and continue to compete.
Dieticians can play an important role in supporting general practitioners and athletes by doing
a full dietary analysis to help make recommendations for short, medium and long-term health and
training goals.
So, we will start off by looking at a case study of an athlete training for a trail marathon.
The athlete wanted to assess his macro and micro nutrients to ensure he was obtaining
good nutrition. Based on his training regimen, we calculated that his daily caloric intake
should be between 3060 and 3363 K-Cals, which was higher than what he was currently taking
As far as macronutrients, we found that he needed to increase his intake of carbohydrates
and lower his intake of fats.
When we looked at vitamin and mineral intake, it was mostly meeting the required levels
apart from vitamin D.
So we recommend...
Question 28.
You hear a morning briefing on a ward.
Now read the question.
Okay, so we have a patient who is admitted last night following a visit to the A&E due
to a sudden development of difficulty over speech and weakness in the right arm and leg.
The neurological examination showed an alert patient who could follow some simple commands,
but with severe impairment of word fluency, naming and repetition and severe weakness
of the right upper extremity.
An electrocardiogram revealed atrial fibrillation.
The current diagnosis is acute cerebral infact, but a head CT scan is needed to rule out
an intercerebral hemorrhage and to confirm diagnosis and start therapy.
We also need to get additional laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, glucose,
prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time.
Question 29.
You hear part a training on handovers between nurses.
read the question.
So Dr Alex is here today to present additional information about our system of handover
between nurses.
Thanks for joining us.
Yes, thank you very much for having me.
So as we have seen before, the flow of the handover is patient details, presenting complaint,
significant history, treatment and plan.
Each part of the handover should be brief and relevant.
For example, while going over the presenting complaint, it is not necessary to go into
all of the details on the chart.
You only need to go into details related to the patient's significant medical history.
For example, today around 10am, this patient's breathing became worse than normal.
His wife calls an ambulance.
This patient has a history of emphysema and is under treatment by the respiratory team
and is on home oxygen 24 hours a day.
Now the details that you give while discussing treatment can include what has been done with
the patient as well as any important details, allergies and family dynamics.
Next, we are going to...
Question 30.
You hear a conversation between a GP and a urologist.
Now read the question.
So, Dr. Jones, I'm calling about the patient I'm referring for a neurologic assessment.
Um, yes, Dr. Selamond, is this the patient with the weakness and wasting of the muscles
of his left hand?
Yes, in addition to the wasting of muscles in his left hand, he also has noticed cramps
in his forearm muscles.
The weakness in cramps are most marked after exertion.
I also noticed in his last appointment that he has developed some fasciculation in the
muscles of the upper arms. It is all there in the notes, but I just wanted to touch base
because I am quite concerned about this patient.
Okay, I have seen the latest blood test results. I will give you a call after I conduct my
physical examination. The patient made an appointment for...
What is the end of part B? Now, look at part C.
Part C. In this part of the test, you'll hear two different extracts. Each extract, you'll
hear health professionals talking about aspects of their work.
For questions 31 to 42, choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what
you hear, complete your answers as you listen. Now look at Extract 1. Extract 1
questions 31 to 36. You hear an interview about extended roles and
diatetics. You now have 90 seconds to read questions 31 to 36. This is a
benchmark education solution sample test paper.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
So, I have with me here today Kaylee Flick, a registered dietitian who works at a local
hospital as a critical care dietitian.
Welcome to our program Mrs Flick.
Thank you for having me.
It is a pleasure to be here to talk more about the field of dietetics.
We dietitians are a small profession, so it is particularly important for us to share
our journey to move the profession forward to inspire the next generation of dietitians.
So as I just mentioned, you currently work as a critical care dietitian. Tell us a bit
more about this role and how it shows that the role of dietetics has changed.
Yes, so as a critical care dietitian, I work as part of a care team providing care for critically
ill patients. This includes identifying patients at nutritional risk, advising on evidence-based
nutritional treatment plans and making decisions about feeding methods.
Nowadays many dieticians are playing extended roles within clinical practice.
Many roles that were traditionally held by nursing or medical professionals are now held
by dieticians working beyond their recognised scope of practice.
Hmm, interesting, so what has given rise to this change?
Originally came about as part of an effort to modernise the NHS and to transform healthcare
services. This involved extended roles for some allied health professionals such as dieticians.
We have seen that it has boosted job satisfaction, improved the dietetic profile,
enhanced multidisciplinary team learning and most of all it has provided better patient care.
It is important to remember that allied health professionals are the third largest workforce
within the NHS. So it is important to look for ways to develop more advanced clinical practice
posts that take advantage of their expertise and skills.
So, with these extended roles, are dieticians working with more complex cases?
Yes, we are certainly seeing dieticians take on more advanced practice. A couple of months
ago there was a patient at my hospital whose care team included two specialised dieticians,
that worked in the ICU and the other one was a bariatric dietitian. Patient who had had
bariatric surgery eight years ago was in a car accident. The ICU dietitian completed
an initial assessment and made decisions about the feeding options and the bariatric dietitian
was called in as an expert on filling and adjusting gastric bands.
That is so interesting. I would never have thought that dietitians would be involved
with those aspects of patient care.
About 20 years ago, it wouldn't have been the case.
These complex cases and expanded roles of dietitians are part of the reason the British
Dietetic Association has taken the important step of putting together four pillars of practice
that all advanced practitioners must take into account as they develop throughout their career.
It is great to hear there is some framework to guide this transition into advanced practice.
Can you tell us a bit more about these pillars?
Of course.
So, the first pillar is Advanced Dietetic Practice, and it refers to the demonstration
of expert knowledge and skills and the management of a complex caseload.
The next pillar is related to research and evidence-based practice, and third pillar encompasses
leadership and management.
As an important part of a multidisciplinary team, it is necessary for dietitians to demonstrate
the capacity for shared leadership. Yes, I would say that is an important competency
for all healthcare professionals. Yes, of course. And the final pillar is related to
education and facilitating learning. Dieticians should facilitate the learning of others,
actively contribute to specialist groups and undertake professional development,
such as including reflection and feedback in their practice. Of course, the contributions
from each pillar will vary depending on the type of job a dietitian holds such as clinical,
research or work in the private sector. So what is next in extending roles for dietitians?
While there has been a change in the way that the NHS thinks of allied health professionals,
there is still a lack of funding for dietitians in many areas of clinical practice.
Despite evidence of the benefits of having a dietitian as part of the critical care team,
No unit in the UK has full-time dietitians.
The same as seen in Australia and New Zealand,
where only 25% of units have weekly dietetic hours.
As you can see, adequate funding is required to ensure
consistent and established dietetic input.
I see, as with many other areas of healthcare.
Now look at X-Track 2.
X-Track 2.
Questions 37-42.
You hear a presentation about the role of general practitioners in the care of older
adults.
You now have 90 seconds to read questions 37 to 42.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
Hello everyone, first of all thank you very much for attending this session on the role
of general practitioners in the care of older adults. As we all know all too well, general
practitioners and their practices are facing unprecedented challenges relating to staff
burnout, finances and an increased workload. Today I'm going to present research highlighting
the challenges that general practitioners face, as well as the importance of general practitioners
in the care of adults.
To start off, I'm going to give an introduction to the study.
So serious infections diagnosed in adults age 65 and over are the leading cause of hospital
admissions and are associated with high mortality.
Detecting the presence of serious infections in older patients is often difficult due to
a variety of reasons.
atypical presentations and non-specific signs of infection. For these reasons and others
that we will explore in a moment, distinguishing which older patients have serious infections
remains an important challenge for general practitioners. In order to better understand
the issues that general practitioners are dealing with in this area, we conducted a
research project that involved doing interviews with 28 different general practitioners and
and analyzing the themes that came up.
The GPs interviewed represented a variety of experience levels, GP roles and practice
populations, interviews involving discussing patients as well as general observations about
a variety of topics.
The first theme involved challenges that lead to diagnostic uncertainty.
The first of these challenges identified was patient complexity.
GPs described how assessing acute illness in older people was frequently confounded by
the background of multiple complex medical and social needs.
For example, several GPs mentioned how multi-morbidity and polypharmacy could affect interpretation
of assessment.
As one GP said, a tachycardia which would be a measure in many other patients isn't
a very good thing if someone's on beta blockers or if they have a pacemaker. Another aspect
of this theme is the lack of knowledge of the patient.
GPs cited the lack of sufficient background information or perceived lack of continuity
as a particular challenge in this context. GPs reported the importance of knowing how
well a person is getting around, whether they're talking the same way, whether they're confused
more, among other changes in a patient's condition, and said that it has become more
difficult to know their patients well. This was particularly relevant for local GPs.
One GP mentioned the increases in GP workload as a barrier to following up with patients.
This pressure on GP's time has also greatly reduced the capacity for home visiting.
Another theme that emerged were approaches to recognise suspected serious infection in
older adults.
One sub-theme here is the difficulty with obtaining patient history as older patients can sometimes
experience confusion or dementia or there can be challenges with communicating with older
patients.
GPs also reported difficulties with relying on vital signs in older patients.
For example, while a high temperature would confirm infection to a GP, a low or normal
temperature was not necessarily reassuring.
Similarly, GP's reported relying on different signs to detect infection in older patients,
such as respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, among others, and not always feeling that
any of the methods were particularly reassuring.
When it came to managing diagnostic uncertainty, GPs reported ordering a wide variety of investigations
with different levels of perceived reliability.
For example, the use of urine dipstick testing was widely reported but interpretation was
often problematic, particularly in catheterized patients.
In addition, the practicalities involved in obtaining some tests limited their use.
One GP said that if she wanted blood tests, she knew it would be a day or two for the
blood to get drawn, and then another day or two for the results to come through.
This delay often resulted in GP's making decisions without getting blood tests.
In conclusion, challenges to diagnosing older people with serious infections are present
at each stage of the patient assessment, such as taking medical history, which is frequently
disrupted by communication difficulties due in part to cognitive impairment and confusion,
as well as during the physical examination, which is not believed to reliably predict
the severity of disease in this age group.
Another conclusion of this study is the impact of losing continuity of care for older patients.
research has shown that long-term high-quality primary care relationship is particularly
important for this age group, especially when it comes to decreasing emergency department
visits and unplanned hospital admissions.
